0f9890a728a058e8.content_excerpt: What a 35-point benchmark cliff, a slowdown study nobody wanted to publish, and real 2026 payroll data say about replacing engineers with agents Claude Opus 4.8 clears 88.6% on SWE-bench Verified . That's the number everyone quotes to argue AI has basically solved software engineering. Now drop it into SWE-bench Pro — the version built from private codebases the model has never seen. The best standardized score on the public leaderboard is 59.1%. On the truly private commercial set, where nobody gets to tune in advance, no model clears 47%. That's not a rounding error. That's a 20-to-40-point cliff, and it shows up everywhere. Gemini 3.1 Pro falls from 80.6% to somewhere between 32% and 46%, depending on which cut you trust. Every lab's flagship shows the same shape of fall. Here's a wrinkle nobody saw coming: the two highest-scoring models that exist right now — Claude Mythos 5 (95.5%) and Claude Fable 5 (95.0%) — aren't something you can actually use. Anthropic suspended public access to both under an export control directive. The "best" model on paper this week is one you can't buy. That gap, between the benchmark you can quote and the codebase you actually own, is the entire "AI replaces developers" argument in miniature. Models are extraordinary at problems that resemble what they've already seen. However, if you run /rename with no arguments, Codex immediately makes an LLM call requesting a title suggestion. 18df784100d9cc05.content_excerpt: A coding-agent CLI can feel quick in a terminal and still be expensive when a workflow starts it in a fresh container for every job. We measured that cost for six CLIs: start-up, time per turn, memory, image size and tokens. On overhead per job, pi was the lightest overall. Our own CLI, aictrl , won no metric but came second on four: session time, harness time per turn, memory and image size. Overhead is half the answer: this experiment does not measure whether an agent completes the task, which our next run will. Goose had the fastest observed median first response, followed by Codex, pi and aictrl. Those four were within 187 ms of each other. pi used the fewest tokens, both in its first request and for a whole short task, spent the least time between model turns, added the least image footprint and finished the scripted session fastest. aictrl came second on session time, per-turn harness time, memory and image footprint. Its system prompt is now as small as pi's. Its tool definitions are not. Each chart is sorted from lowest to highest, with gold and silver medals for the observed first and second place on that metric. A medal describes this experiment; small gaps do not establish a stable lead. Disclosure: I build aictrl. This article reports our own measurements, including where our implementation loses. 30905c664e5a48e8.content_excerpt: ARD is an open discovery protocol for agentic resources ( GitHub ). It allows an AI client to ask: "What is available for this task?" and lets a discovery service answer with matching resources. ARD sits entirely before invocation. It helps the client find the right resource; the resource is then invoked through its own native mechanism. An agentic resource is any external capability an AI client can call on to do a task — an agent, MCP server, Skill, Canvas, Plugin, API, or workflow — anything that can be described as an ARD entry . It is not an execution runtime: ARD is not MCP, A2A, Skills, AI Catalog, or an API runtime, and it does not replace them. It is not a central catalog: There will be many discovery services, each indexing different resources, serving different communities, and applying its own trust, ranking, and access policies. Every enterprise can run its own — much like an intranet has its own search engine over internal content. And on the public web there will be many, some optimizing for quality and trust, others for coverage. ARD is being developed by a working group with participants from Microsoft, Google, Hugging Face, GoDaddy, and others. This work is part of a broader effort to create an open discovery layer for resources that AIs can draw on. Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) and its resources are licensed under the Apache License 2.0 and welcomes contributions from the community.

4eb8a6cb7861fe9d.content_excerpt: QwenPU is Qwen3.5-4B with a 32-bit RISC-V CPU and a vector unit compiled into its weights. The vector unit runs a whole neural network inside the model's forward passes: Andrej Karpathy's stories260K , the 260K-parameter Llama from llama2.c , runs as a program on it and writes its stories. It's part of Qwenputer : the same CPU, compiled into transformer layers in front of Qwen's own, every weight set by a compiler, with Qwen3.5's Gated DeltaNet state as its memory. Qwenputer-npu gave that CPU dot-product instructions. QwenPU gives it a vector unit of its own: separate memories in DeltaNet heads, 64-lane matrix rows a token, and whole vector results streamed through the token stream. Work in progress. QwenPU is exact, but not yet small: the checkpoint is 26.7 GB, so it needs a 40 GB or larger GPU to load whole. The story demo and the checks run the computer's layers on their own and fit a 24 GB GPU. Trimming the hidden size, and with it the checkpoint, is next. stories260K is a C program here ( guests/stories260k/stories_vx.c ). Its int4 weights sit in the vector unit's weight memory, loaded from the program, and every matrix row, residual add, softmax and attention read is a vector op. None of it is compiled into the checkpoint, so any model that fits runs the same way. Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. One day, she saw a big, red ball. She wanted to play with it, but it was too high Its memories are DeltaNet heads: 1

5b44a10be2d2e731.content_excerpt: To write this issue, we asked a coding agent to add email invitations and an audit log to a small TypeScript app , then reviewed the pull request (PR) it produced. It came to 31 files and about 1,700 changed lines, with a two-sentence description. GitHub listed the files alphabetically, so the review opened on a CI config change, and the migration every other file depended on sat below five API files. PRs this size are becoming routine. At Rails World in September, David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH) said 37signals now has agents writing nearly all of its code. Generating code is now cheap, and the human attention needed to review it is what runs out. Thanks for reading ByteSizedBets! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work. Keeping PRs small is still the best fix. Agents don’t reliably do it, though, and some changes are large by nature, like a schema migration or a rename across the whole repo. This issue is about reviewing those well. We also planted nine problems in the PR, from a privilege escalation to a behavior change hidden inside a moved file, so we could see what the tooling caught and what it missed. The walkthrough below uses CodeRabbit Explain , and every screenshot comes from that PR. Where plain git covers part of the job, I’ve included the commands. GitHub’s diff view works well for small changes a person wrote. On our PR, it fell short in four ways. Files are sorted alphabetically, which has nothing to do with how the change was built. On our

967be99077d13f07.content_excerpt: One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based. Frameworks are “blazing fast,” tools will “supercharge” your development, the right abstraction will benefit both you and your users ( DX and UX all in one!). All of this breathless boasting is usually offered with zero evidence. Alex Russell has called this “frontend’s lost decade” , Baldur Bjarnason has called programming a pop culture , and I’ve tried to counter this trend in my blog with facts and benchmarks (at my best, anyway). For a long time it seemed like our community’s allergy to evidence was driven by the desire for greater DX . In other words, devs just liked the way it felt to type JSX in React, and the arguments promoting React or related tools (“the virtual DOM is fast!”) were largely post-hoc rationalizations to justify those initial gut feelings. ( Jonathan Haidt would likely agree with this assessment.) But in the agentic era, when developers are no longer typing code by hand and are thus less constrained by DX, I still see vibes ruling the day (and not just in the sense of “vibe-coding”). Frontends are rewritten because some framework or another is “better for agents.” (Did anyone think to ask the agents?) The resulting code is “faster,” the agents make “fewer mistakes,” etc. Once again, these claims are often made without evidence. b78023b26122d472.content_excerpt: Claude Haiku scored 82% on 21 MCP servers through OpenCode and 65% through Claude Code. The gap comes from the built-in tools each agent reaches for first. We ran the same model, Claude Haiku 5.5, through two coding agents against the same 21 MCP servers, with the agent as the only difference. Through OpenCode it answered 82.0% of the tasks correctly from the server. Through Claude Code it answered 65.4%. We were testing M3 , our open-source tool for testing MCP servers , and wanted a workload big enough to break it: 21 real servers, about 20 tasks each, three agents, three trials per task. The results became the MCP Agent Usability leaderboard , and every number in this post comes from it. Our first guess was that OpenCode is simply better at calling tools. Splitting the servers by what they do rules that out. Eleven of the servers do a job none of the agents has a built-in tool for: a Postgres database, MongoDB, Redis, Kafka, Linear, Jenkins, Grafana, Kubernetes, Gitea, and two browser servers. The other ten overlap with something every agent already carries: web search and docs lookup (Exa, Fetch, Microsoft Learn, DeepWiki, Terraform), files and shell (Git, Filesystem, Desktop Commander, Serena), and memory. On the first eleven, the three agents land within 4.1 points of each other, even though Codex runs a different model. baaa37d6dddd5d25.content_excerpt: Deterministic code dictionary for LLMs and developers: tree-sitter + SQLite, no AI. Cuts Claude Code token use by answering code questions from an index. A dictionary of your code for the AI, and a manual for you. It reads your project once, with no AI, and hands the answer over together with the question. Fewer turns, fewer tokens, the same correct answer. One line, once per machine. It also turns codedict on in Claude Code for every project. That's it. Open Claude Code in any git repository and ask about the code. There is nothing else to configure. Uninstall: run ~/.codedict/venv/bin/python -m codedict setup --remove (Windows: ~\.codedict\venv\Scripts\python.exe -m codedict setup --remove ) and delete the ~/.codedict folder. codedict came from a practical problem: on a real project with ~250 files in TypeScript, C# and Python, Claude Code sessions kept hitting the usage limit. We measured it, and the culprit was not the code being read but the number of turns . Every time the AI calls a tool (a grep, opening a file), Claude Code re-reads the whole context: 35 to 50 thousand tokens per turn. A simple question like "where is X and who calls it?" took 5 turns of grep and file reads. A flow question like "from the click to the result" took more than 20. The idea was to do the search work once, with no AI , in a local index, and hand the ready answer over together with the question. The AI answers in 1 or 2 turns instead of 5 to 20. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks. Every MCP tool call dumps raw data into your context window. A Playwright snapshot costs 56 KB. Twenty GitHub issues cost 59 KB. One access log — 45 KB. After 30 minutes, 40% of your context is gone. And when the agent compacts the conversation to free space, it forgets which files it was editing, what tasks are in progress, and what you last asked for. On top of that, the agent wastes output tokens on filler, pleasantries, and verbose explanations — burning context from both sides. Context Saving — Sandbox tools keep raw data out of the context window. 315 KB becomes 5.4 KB. 98% reduction. Session Continuity — Every file edit, git operation, task, error, and user decision is tracked in SQLite. When the conversation compacts, context-mode doesn't dump this data back into context — it indexes events into FTS5 and retrieves only what's relevant via BM25 search. The model picks up exactly where you left off. If you don't --continue , previous session data is deleted immediately — a fresh session means a clean slate. Think in Code — The LLM should program the analysis, not compute it. Instead of reading 50 files into context to count functions, the agent writes a script that does the counting and console.log() s only the result. One script replaces ten tool calls and saves 100x context. This is a mandatory para

dbaecb6c683e8493.content_excerpt: Adversarial agent loops (producer, worker, gatekeeper) so agents do routine work and humans make the key decisions devloops gives a coding agent three loops: producer , worker , and gatekeeper . Each loop is a skill ( SKILL.md plus helper scripts). You install the skills into a project's .agents/skills/ directory. A per-project file, devloops.config.yaml , holds the project values (repo, branches, commands, protected paths, labels). Most maintenance work is routine: find a problem, write an issue, fix it, review the fix. devloops lets agents do that routine work in an adversarial loop : The worker and the gatekeeper go back and forth until the gatekeeper approves. The human does not do this routine work. The human makes only the important decisions: A scheduler starts each loop in ticks . Before a worker tick starts the agent, tick_gate.py decides if there is anything to do: So a change that happens during a tick is never hidden, and only an idle, unchanged state gives NOOP . The producer has its own gate, producer_gate.py . It picks the most overdue task ( --next ) from the task periods in the config. It does not overwrite a skill that already exists. Add the state directory (default .devloops/ ) to .gitignore . Check the prerequisites first (Python, GitHub API, git , gh auth , push permission): /gatekeeper-loop and /producer-loop use the same forms. /gatekeeper-loop 10m --pr N reviews one PR. /producer-loop runs one producer task. e7aea804d1201fff.content_excerpt: Every few months, someone points out that the world is drowning in idle compute. Your laptop idles at an office desk. Your phone spends most of its battery waiting in your pocket. Meanwhile, tech monopolies pour hundreds of billions of dollars into sprawling, water-guzzling data centers packed with high-end clusters to train and run modern language models. The intuitive alternative is obvious: split the model up and run it across everyone’s devices. Yet whenever people attempt decentralized AI, they run into the same brick wall. Projects like Petals and BloomBee proved you could run inference over the public internet, but they mostly approach it through pipeline parallelism—handing entire layers to individual machines. The trouble with that strategy is the entry fee. If Layer 14 requires 8 GB or 16 GB of memory, every device with only 2 GB or 4 GB of spare RAM gets locked out. The network ends up looking like a rickety chain of modest servers rather than a truly universal computing mesh. The real breakthrough isn’t distributing layer by layer. It is slicing within the sub-layers themselves. A standard Transformer block is made of two distinct computational engines: the feed-forward / MLP block and the attention mechanism. For a visual way to picture what changes as information passes through those blocks, I explored that in The words are the shadow . Here, the question is how to split that computation across devices.
